clue.text: Football hooligan does damage to Liverpool, say

parts.note: to spoil something is to damage or ruin it
Liverpool is an example of a port, a city on the sea where ships dock

explanation.surface: A thug at a match causes trouble for Liverpool's football team.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Liverpool' looks like the football club, but here it is just an example of a seaport. The definition is playful: a hooligan ruins the game for everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: A person who ruins other people's fun or game is a killjoy, and a hooligan at a match does exactly that.

clue.text: Not all are like this to me

parts.note: so means in this way or like this
taken as written

explanation.surface: A remark that only a few people feel this way towards the speaker.
explanation.definitionFit: A part rather than the whole: a few or a portion, not every one.

clue.text: Watchful braves not taken by surprise

indicators.note: being caught off guard throws these letters into disorder, so they are rearranged

explanation.surface: Alert warriors who were not caught off guard.
explanation.definitionFit: Being alert and noticing what goes on around you is the same as keeping a careful watch.

clue.text: Free to be at it — that's great!

explanation.surface: Someone exults at being allowed to do something.
explanation.walkthrough: The first definition is a phrase with a gap: a person who is free is 'at' this word, as in an escaped prisoner being at large.
explanation.definitionFit: An escaped convict 'at large' is loose and unconfined; separately the word means big or sizeable.

clue.text: Some charge put on wine

parts.note: port is a fortified wine from Portugal
an ion is an atom carrying an electric charge

explanation.surface: A price added to the cost of a bottle of wine.
explanation.walkthrough: 'charge' suggests a fee, but it is the electrically charged particle; 'put on' just says it is added after the wine.
explanation.definitionFit: A share or part of something is some of it rather than all of it.

clue.text: Draws attention to collecting box and disconcerts people

explanation.surface: A charity collector shakes a tin and unsettles passers-by.
explanation.walkthrough: A street collector for charity shakes a coin tin to get noticed; the word also means unnerves or flusters.
explanation.definitionFit: A collector shakes coins noisily in a tin to be noticed, and to unnerve someone is to fluster them.

clue.text: Smart fellow the French take into account

indicators.note: the French article is placed within the abbreviation for account, as if taken inside it

parts.note: le is French for the

explanation.surface: A clever man has French people consider him in their reckoning.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition relies on the phrase 'smart alec', a know-all.
explanation.definitionFit: A boy's name that completes the idiom for a cocky know-all, a clever-clogs.

clue.text: Their girders are primed

parts.note: read 'girders' not as steel beams but as people who gird, as in the biblical command to gird up a part of the body before action

explanation.surface: Steel beams on a building site have been painted with primer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Girders' looks like building beams; it means those who gird, and 'primed' means ready for action, as in the old phrase about girding up before a task.
explanation.definitionFit: The lower back and hips are what one girds up, in the biblical idiom, before setting to work.

clue.text: Harmony in a musical instrument

parts.note: concert means agreement or harmony, as in acting in concert
taken as written

explanation.surface: Melodious sound produced by an instrument.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Harmony' suggests music, but it means agreement, as in acting 'in concert'.
explanation.definitionFit: A small hexagonal squeezebox with bellows and buttons is a type of musical instrument.

clue.text: NUT ruined anything not affected by their members?

indicators.note: the letters of the word in capitals are wrecked and so rearranged

parts.note: aught is an old word for anything at all

explanation.surface: A broken nut, and things that its parts do not influence.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ruined' turns NUT into UNT. The definition is loose: people uninfluenced by the members of a teaching staff have had no instruction.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone never instructed has not been shaped by any teacher or schooling.

clue.text: He keeps on accumulating endless unhappiness

indicators.note: without its end means the last letter of the synonym is dropped

parts.note: misery is deep unhappiness

explanation.surface: Someone who keeps piling up sorrow without pause.
explanation.walkthrough: 'endless' looks like it describes everlasting sorrow, but it removes the final Y of MISERY.
explanation.definitionFit: A hoarder who keeps amassing money without spending is a skinflint.

clue.text: Enter into arrangement for storage

indicators.note: an arrangement of these letters means they are put in a new order

explanation.surface: Sign up to a scheme for keeping things in a warehouse.
explanation.definitionFit: Keeping or holding something is the act of storing it.

clue.text: You do what you like with it

definitions.text: You do what you like with it

parts.words: You do what you like with it
parts.note: a description of the human faculty of choosing for oneself, phrased like a remark about an object handed over

explanation.surface: Someone handing over an object says it is yours to use as you please.
explanation.walkthrough: The 'it' seems to be a thing given away, but it is the faculty of choice that lets you act as you wish.
explanation.definitionFit: The power to choose one's actions freely is what lets a person act as they wish.

clue.text: A short island passage

parts.note: an isle is a small island, and the word is also a shortened form

explanation.surface: A brief route across a small island.
explanation.definitionFit: A gangway between rows of seats, as in a church or theatre, is a passage.

clue.text: A sphere lacking reality

parts.note: sphere read as a realm or world, and lacking reality as imaginary, as in sleep or fantasy

explanation.surface: A globe that does not really exist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sphere' suggests a ball, but it is a realm, and one that is imaginary is a fantasy land.
explanation.definitionFit: An imaginary realm of fantasy, detached from real life, is a place one only conjures up.

clue.text: Dress again in regal fashion

indicators.note: to fashion is to shape or make, so these letters are reshaped

explanation.surface: Putting on clothes once more in a royal style.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dress' looks like clothing but is the military sense of lining up troops in straight rows.
explanation.definitionFit: To dress ranks is to line them up straight, so to dress again is to put back into line.

clue.text: Any in, let out, naturally

indicators.note: out signals that the letters are thrown into disorder and rearranged

explanation.surface: Anyone admitted, then released, as a matter of course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'out' and 'in' look like opposites in the surface, but 'out' alone is the anagram signal on ANY IN LET.
explanation.definitionFit: Something done by inborn nature happens instinctively, without being learned.

clue.text: Division has key-men mounted outside

indicators.note: the word for mounted surrounds the other piece, sitting outside it

parts.note: a jewel that is mounted is set in its fitting
G is a musical key, followed by men

explanation.surface: A department where the important staff are positioned on horses outside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'key-men' looks like essential staff; it is the musical key G plus MEN, which SET (mounted, as a gem) wraps around.
explanation.definitionFit: A section or part into which something is split is one division of it.

clue.text: Newspaper boss put thought into words

parts.note: the Daily Express is a British national newspaper
ED is short for editor, the boss of a paper

explanation.surface: A newspaper's chief writes his ideas down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Newspaper boss' reads as one person, but it is two pieces: the Express, a British tabloid, and ED, short for editor.
explanation.definitionFit: To voice or state an idea is to put it into language.

clue.text: About ten Anna's a bit of a butterfly

indicators.note: about means around or in disorder, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: the name Anna as written, the possessive adding no letter

explanation.surface: A girl called Anna, aged about ten, is something of a social butterfly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'About ten' seems to give Anna's age; 'About' is the anagram signal for TEN ANNA. The definition is a feeler on a butterfly's head.
explanation.definitionFit: A butterfly's head carries a pair of slender feelers, each one part of the insect.

clue.text: There's no accounting for his performance

definitions.text: There's no accounting for his performance

parts.words: There's no accounting for his performance
parts.note: read 'no accounting' literally: nobody pays or bills for this person's playing, since they are unpaid

explanation.surface: A remark that someone's poor showing is beyond explanation.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'there's no accounting for' means it cannot be explained; read literally, no money changes hands because the performer is unpaid.
explanation.definitionFit: A performer who does it for love, without a fee, is a non-professional.

clue.text: One's behind a way to delay action

explanation.surface: Someone is slow off the mark and puts things off.
explanation.walkthrough: 'behind' looks like lagging, but it is the backside, humorously named as the part one sits on; to sit on a matter is to delay acting on it.
explanation.definitionFit: A jocular term for the buttocks, and sitting on a proposal means holding it back.

clue.text: Retire from the contest -not up to it?

explanation.surface: A competitor withdraws because they are not good enough.
explanation.walkthrough: The second definition fills a gap: something 'not up to' this word is below standard.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse withdrawn before a race is struck off; the idiom 'not up to the mark' means below standard.

clue.text: Best, strange as it seems

parts.note: best read as a verb, to beat or outdo, which has a synonym that looks like its opposite

explanation.surface: Admitting that the top result is odd.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Best' looks like the superlative; as a verb it means defeat, and its synonym oddly looks like the opposite of best.
explanation.definitionFit: To get the better of an opponent is to defeat them, oddly expressed by the word for the lowest.

clue.text: Fleet Street contains an awful mixture of printers

indicators.note: the abbreviation for street holds the other letters inside it

parts.note: RD is short for road, a street
an gives A, the indefinite article
pi is printers' jargon for jumbled type

explanation.surface: London's newspaper district holds a dreadful jumble of print workers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fleet Street' looks like the London home of newspapers; 'Fleet' is the definition. 'pi' (or pie) is a printers' term for a heap of mixed-up type.
explanation.definitionFit: Fleet as an adjective means swift or quick-moving.

clue.text: Held in apprehension?

parts.note: apprehension read as being caught by police, not as fear

explanation.surface: Someone gripped by anxiety.
explanation.walkthrough: 'apprehension' looks like dread, but it is also the act of catching a suspect.
explanation.definitionFit: A suspect apprehended by police has been detained in custody.

clue.text: Resort to Sergeant-Major to get fit

parts.note: a spa is a health resort

explanation.surface: Going to a drill instructor to get into shape.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Resort to' looks like 'turn to', and 'fit' like healthy; 'fit' is a sudden convulsion.
explanation.definitionFit: A sudden seizure or convulsion is a fit, as in a coughing fit.

clue.text: Finishes off objectives

explanation.surface: Someone completes their goals.
explanation.definitionFit: To finish is to conclude, and aims or goals are the purposes one works towards.

clue.text: It's revolting, drive away fast!

parts.note: to repel is to force back or drive off
Lent is the Christian season of fasting

explanation.surface: A disgusting thing prompts someone to shoo it away quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fast' looks like quickly, but it is a period of abstaining, Lent.
explanation.definitionFit: Something disgusting or offensive repels people.

clue.text: The offence of one coming to light

definitions.text: The offence of one coming to light

parts.words: The offence of one coming to light
parts.note: coming to light read as setting things alight, not as being discovered

explanation.surface: A crime that is uncovered.
explanation.walkthrough: 'coming to light' suggests discovery; read literally it means bringing something to a flame.
explanation.definitionFit: The crime of deliberately setting property on fire.

clue.text: They may be put on but don't go off

explanation.surface: Things that are applied but never activate.
explanation.walkthrough: The first sense is slang for clothes, which are put on; the second is shells or bombs that fail to explode.
explanation.definitionFit: Informal clothes are worn, and failed shells are those that never explode.

clue.text: Mathematician made riches in a way

indicators.note: in a different way means the letters are put into a new order

explanation.surface: A mathematician got rich after a fashion.
explanation.definitionFit: The ancient Greek scholar of Syracuse famous for geometry and the principle of buoyancy.
